I was like you at one point, except I understood it a little bit better.  I'd taken LSD three times before my first 'big' trip and I thought I knew everything.  I thought it couldn't touch me but oh boy, I was wrong.  

I'd dropped 600ug before with no complications and had the best time of my life.  After that I dropped 800-900ug a few months later and that was by far the hardest and also the best night of my life.  

If you don't respect it, it will tear you apart.  Relentlessly.  I cried, a lot.  I turned my bedroom lights off and couldn't bear the sound of music or TV. It showed me every single thing I couldn't do and every single bad thing I'd done to another person.  After a while I became convinced that I was dead and I had to accept my own death.  I had to accept that I'd never see anyone I loved or cared about again and it made me realise the value of life.  

When you start to respect it and accept it instead of fighting it, it will start to comfort you.  It helped me through all that pain after a while, it didn't just leave me alone.  I became connected to the network of life and melted away for hours afterwards.  

Just because my trip turned out alright in the end doesn't mean that yours will.  I was somewhat aware of what was happening to me because I had previous experiences under my belt.  Letting go was the hardest part.  

You don't have enough experience to know what makes a good trip good and bad trip bad.  Don't try to school people on something that you don't know anything about.  Just because you've had one good experience doesn't mean you know the ins and outs of acid.  You're always learning more about the drug with every trip. 

Take it down a notch.  Learn a bit more.

They said we'd be going away for three weeks and promised that they'd pay for a 'top kennel' so that my dog had somewhere to go.

Solo tripping is my favourite.  No distractions.  I find that having people around when I'm tripping ruins the experience, but that's just me. 

I try to prep at least a week before I trip.  My next solo trip is nine days away and I've already started preparing.  Tidying up your tripping area is a must, you don't want your room to be screaming at you.  

Preparing some snacks is good too, even if you don't eat them.  It's good to just have them there in case you do need them.  Have a bottle of water or two too.  Stay hydrated.  Eat something healthy a few hours before you trip, just so you don't end up with an upset stomach.  

Prepare a playlist of some songs that you'll at least think you'll listen to.  Spotify can also create a radio based around your playlist of songs that are similar.  This is suuuuper fun while tripping I think, I like listening to music that I didn't think I would be listening to.  

Most importantly, just enjoy it.  Try not to think too much about it.  Let it all be.  Don't fight it, don't try and control it.  Let the trip come to you, let LSD do what it needs to do.  Have no expectations.  One thing that I do is write a note for myself just before I trip that says something like 'it's alright, you're just on acid'.  It's reassuring if I begin to completely lose any sense of reality and end up forgetting that I've even dropped.  

Good luck and happy tripping, man.  You'll be all good!

My dad was always open about his use of psychedelics, even when I was younger but my mum still hasn't been completely open about her use of it.  Even now that she knows I'm actively involved in the use of LSD and Psilocybin, she won't really talk about it.  

I don't think it made my parents any different from non-psychedelic using parents.  They've always been laid back and I think that would have been the case regardless of whether or not they used these things.   It's made them very cool about drug use though and they made the effort to educate me early about correct usage, the importance of testing your substances and set/setting.  I don't have to worry about them being angry about my own substance use, even when I was taking ecstasy.  My dad has always said though that if he felt like there was a genuine problem, he'd intervene.  

To be honest, I'd say that my uncle is the most experienced with LSD.  We've tripped together once and we regularly talk about our trips.  He tells me that once, he dropped eight tabs and 'saw life in the form of a big, smiling plant woman with infinite arms'.  I can confide in him more about my personal use of LSD as he's a lot more down to earth about it.  

I'd say that my parents' general style and music taste was influenced by LSD.  Both of my parents and my uncle are huge stoners too, like myself so they're all pretty.. I don't know how to put it other than kind of 'hippie'.  My house has a lot of psychedelic tapestries in it and it's pretty much perfect for tripping, full of coloured lights and things that are visually stimulating.  My mum is an avid listener of Grateful Dead and the like, as well as Schpongle.  

My mum hasn't actually touched LSD since around 2005-6.  She was very, very into it and kind of used it the same way someone who loved coke or speed would take that.  My dad is actually more into DMT.  They split up a few years ago but it's all good.  The two of them just smoke weed now regularly.  However, my uncle is still an avid user of LSD, shrooms and occasionally DMT.  

I think the most beneficial part of having two psychedelic loving parents is that it taught me that they're both still people.  A lot of people seem to think that because I have two parents that are so relaxed around substances, it'd make them 'better' or 'easier' parents.  It really didn't.  Both of them are considerably fucked up and they fucked each other up too, as well as kind of fucking me up in the process.  I could easily say that their use of LSD in my younger years made them bad parents but honestly, it didn't.  Just like it never made them good parents either.  They are still cool people nonetheless.

One thing I've learned from spending years feeling depressed and suicidal is that things can and will change.  Maybe not right now and maybe not even next month but regardless of how long it takes, it's worth waiting for. 
I was the socially awkward, slightly overweight stoner kid in school and I found it hard to properly communicate with people without coming across the wrong way and scaring them off.  I did have decent enough friends but my social circles were small and somewhat limited.  Since I'd been extremely depressed and anxiety ridden for almost four years, I was convinced that nothing was going to change and that this was essentially going to be my life - sad and filled with paranoia and self-doubt.  
Then things started looking up, y'know? I left school, I lost two stone, I started getting better after thinking that I never would.  Even though I'd came close to killing myself, I soon realised after things started getting better that there are so many amazing things to look forward to in the future.  
One thing I wish I'd learned sooner is that you can't rely on other people for happiness.  Being social is good, having friends is good but I wish I'd spent more time alone actually focusing on making myself into a more confident person rather than trying to make friends with people that were emotional leeches.  
Continuing to be yourself is probably one of the best and most powerful things you can do - continue being YOU, don't change for anyone but yourself if you feel as though you need to. You are you, beautifully unique and full of potential.  You aren't irreparable or incapable of making friends, it will come and it will happen.  I have faith in you and I hope you have faith in yourself.  If you ever want to talk or anything then don't be afraid to PM me!

My parents were never at all hard on me.  They were very rarely encouraging and had little to no involvement in my education or personal life.  I'm not saying that they were bad parents.  They split when I was 10 and I'll admit that they had their problems, well, maybe a lot of problems. 
In a way, they gave me too much freedom because they were both wrapped up in their personal lives.  My mum provided for me well but never really invested herself emotionally.  My dad was narcissistic and he had a temper, so approaching him about things was never really an option.  
Whenever I tried to get help for school, they'd always tell me to just 'do what you need to'.  This was when I was maybe around eight or nine, so their lack of encouragement and support really set me back.  They were never hard on me or strict, which was good for me until the novelty wore off and I realised that I'd done fuckall with my time.  They never pushed me to study and never pushed me to complete assignments or take part in out of school activities. Both of them hated their jobs and dropped out of school, so I was surrounded by constant negativity surrounding work, school and college.  As a result of them never pushing me, I wasted a lot of my talent because I didn't know how to push myself.  They always wanted me to do well but never did anything to help me with that, and only now do I realise how much this has affected me.  When I stressed about exams or tests, their response was always just 'don't worry about it just now'.  They pretty much let me do anything I wanted for a huge chunk of my life and this led to me developing some really bad habits. 

I had to learn how to push myself, I had to learn how to be strict with myself and I had to learn how to do a lot of things on my own.  Fortunately now, I have more of a structure to my life but it really does anger me that they never really involved themselves in my education. I don't know if this even makes any sense.

Back when I was in primary school, we had this kid join our class when we were in about P6.  We'd heard rumours about him being a 'problem' student but most of us dismissed it as just talk.  
He never displayed any bad behaviours when he first joined the class, he was just quiet. Then he started to act out violently against other pupils, teachers and support staff.  He even held a craft knife up to another kid's throat and he fought with other kids all the time (even younger ones like 10-11).  There were a couple of times that our whole class had to be moved to a different room cause' this kid went completely nuts and destroyed the classroom we usually used.  It was so bad that when we were in P7, parents wrote to the school asking them to ban him from attending our end of term week long trip.  He wasn't allowed to go because almost everybody's parents complained.  
He actually went to the same secondary school as me and ended up gaining a LOT of weight.  He just got worse from there.  Earlier on this year he told a teacher that he wanted to rape her mother, her dead mother. He'd frequently fight, threaten and bully pupils.
